Yes—both exist as experimental, bounded capabilities:

  • Browser playground: interactive WASM experiments for scattering fields, multipole spectra, and gradient-based optimization, plus selected periodic-array and photonic-crystal demos. It exposes a subset of the Python package.
  • GPU support: explicit CUDA paths for dense solves and field evaluation, tested on an RTX 4080 SUPER. Dense solves support pullbacks; the fused field kernel is forward-only. GPU geometry gradients and automatic JAX/PyTorch GPU routing aren’t supported.

text: ok now - what's left for qualification?

items.html: I’ll check the core qualification plan and remaining evidence gaps, keeping the deferred browser and GPU work separate.

The remaining work is qualifying the corrected core on a frozen revision—not adding more features. Linux functional tests, clean-wheel execution, lint/types, and documentation checks already pass.

  1. Prepare both hosts. Sync current main, rerun the core checks on macOS, build optimized extensions, and record fresh source/binary hashes. Update the old campaign helpers to exclude GPU work.
  2. Run the corrected campaign. Start with the Mac regression preflight, then 1,300 Linux cases and 1,294 Mac cases covering accuracy, gradients, runtime, memory, scaling, and numerical boundaries. Neither full corrected campaign has started.
  3. Close the numerical findings. Confirm the metallic-sphere fix across the broader accuracy suite; reconcile high-order cluster/rotation disagreements using independent references. Preserve genuine limitations and failed comparisons.
  4. Verify the performance claims. Measure the proposed dense-memory improvement and check the previously slower Mac cases. Targeted improvements don’t yet establish full-suite results.
  5. Finalize the evidence. Audit coverage and provenance, inspect the generated report, update the qualification claims, and preserve the raw evidence durably—it is currently local/untracked.

Browser/GPU qualification is excluded. Broader platform support, higher derivatives, and additional paper reproductions needn’t block finishing the documented CPU scope.

The concrete checklist is in benchmarks/RESUME.md.

text: ok ignore macos, i want to wrap this up for linux on this machine for now. basically the goal is make sure that everything is correct and at parity right? how do we get there? is there any implementation work remaining or is it really just running a script

items.html: I’ll check the Linux runner and unresolved numerical findings to separate known implementation work from validation that still needs to run.

Mostly qualification work, with a little runner cleanup—not a known backlog of missing solver features. But I can’t promise that no numerical fixes remain until the corrected implementation passes the campaign.

The target should be correctness and numerical/API parity within the documented CPU contract on this Linux machine. Matching upstream alone isn’t enough: upstream has known numerical defects, and our explicit-object API intentionally differs from its ndarray metadata machinery.

I’d finish it in this order:

  1. Make the qualification run self-contained. Remove the old GPU phase from the execution/report helpers, use fresh output directories, and build one optimized version with recorded hashes. Most machinery already exists.
  2. Run correctness first. Upstream comparisons, independent high-precision references, physical invariants, published workflows, full-gradient checks, and the numerical boundary cases. The ordinary Linux tests and clean-wheel checks already pass.
  3. Investigate every failed numerical gate. Fix native defects and add regressions. Where upstream is wrong, retain independent evidence explaining the disagreement rather than weakening tolerances. The metallic-sphere correction and high-order cluster/rotation cases deserve particular attention.
  4. Then finish performance and memory qualification, and publish the final evidence and supported limits. Speedups are a separate claim from correctness.

One important detail: the runner finishing successfully does not mean qualification passed. Some collectors deliberately exit successfully while recording failed comparisons. The result audit must inspect those numerical gates; the existing audit already handles much of this.

So the next step is a Linux correctness run with failure triage, not speculative implementation or immediately launching every timing case. Completion means no unexplained native failures in the declared qualification set, with any exclusions explicitly justified.

text: whats the bottom line on this? what are the changes? would you say this is objectively better? if so, do a last reviews pass and then get these changes into main and push, including documentation on evals

items.html:
Yes—measurably better on the tested agent workflows. Full passes increased 110/120 → 118/120, with 80% fewer nonpasses and 27.4% less observed agent time. The predeclared 40% time-reduction target was not met.

The main changes are:

  • Clear physical constructors and named results, with workflows like response.scatter(incident).efield(points).
  • Consistent Advect/JAX/PyTorch interfaces for sensitivity analysis and optimization.
  • Searchable help and executable examples available directly from the installed wheel.
  • Removal of ambiguous legacy Python names and operations. Rust numerical kernels are unchanged.

The final review fixed polarization handling, negative-index plane-wave behavior, framework cylinder widths, exposed signatures, and a grader filesystem issue.

Verification passed: 93 Rust tests, 2,307 Python tests, 40 plotting/report tests, clean-wheel checks and rustdoc. All 160 saved final submissions retained their outcomes on the reviewed wheel. Solver performance/memory qualification was not rerun; the Advect scalar-input limitation is documented.

Merged and pushed main at 4324000 (now f93276f), including eval results and review evidence. The API branch is also pushed. The completed worktree was removed, with raw evidence preserved. No PR or comments were created.
